title: Images Talk Back: Guiding MMDiTs by Suppressing Image-to-Text Feedback

paper.title: Images Talk Back: Guiding MMDiTs by Suppressing Image-to-Text Feedback
paper.abstract: Abstract Multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs) allow the evolving image to update internal text representations through joint attention. These representations then guide subsequent image updates, raising a question: does this feedback help correct deviations from the prompt, or preserve them? We find that image-to-text (I2T) feedback can preserve the objects and attributes already represented in the evolving image, including errors. Transplanting I2T messages can rescue failures or disrupt successes. At matched intervention strengths, suppressing the influence of I2T feedback improves generation, whereas opposite controls degrade it. These findings motivate Semantic Feedback Guidance (SFG), which suppresses the influence of I2T feedback by guiding away from an auxiliary branch that strengthens this feedback and weakens text-to-image conditioning. The in-place variant, iSFG, directly suppresses I2T feedback and strengthens text-to-image conditioning, requiring no extra model evaluations. Temporal interventions motivate running the SFG branch during the first 20% of image sampling steps, requiring about 1.2 × 1.2\times the base NFE without classifier-free guidance (CFG). Experiments across three image-generation backbones show gains in alignment and preference-model scores. On FLUX, adding SFG to CFG raises GenEval from 0.6661 0.6661 to 0.7479 0.7479 ; on SD3.5M, iSFG adds + 1.33 +1.33 HPSv2.1 over CFG at zero extra NFE. The control also transfers to text-to-video and image-to-video generation, improving VBench scores. Code is available at https://github.com/yyc1215lll-creator/SFG .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text prompts specify what an image generator should produce, but in MMDiTs, the internal text stream also depends on what the model is drawing. Text queries read image keys and values before later blocks use the updated text stream to condition the image. This image-to-text-to-image loop underlies Stable Diffusion 3/3.5, FLUX, Qwen-Image, and HunyuanVideo ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) . When the image departs from the prompt, does this feedback correct the departure or preserve the existing image content? For the prompt “an apple and an orange,” an image containing only an apple may write that incomplete scene back into the text stream. Figure 2 illustrates the two possible effects: recovering the orange or reinforcing its omission. The answer determines whether early errors are corrected or persist through sampling. Figure 2: Image-to-text feedback. The current image writes into internal text states through B i → t B_{i\rightarrow t} , which later blocks read to update the image. If the image misses an object, does this feedback help recover it or preserve the incomplete scene? Text labels and AI-generated fruit images illustrate schematic states and possible outcomes; the input prompt stays fixed. Existing analyses describe the image-to-text path as a register for image content and object identity, or as the weaker cross-modal direction ( Toker et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Shin et al., 2025 ) . They leave open how this content affects generation. We use image content to mean the objects and attributes represented in the evolving image. Such content can conflict with the prompt; we test the effect of preserving it by intervening on this path. To address these questions, we intervene on the image-to-text path and measure its effect on generation. We find that this feedback can preserve image content that conflicts with the prompt, and identify suppression as a useful direction. Specifically, we design two experiments to examine feedback content and local response direction. Message transplantation shows that feedback can rescue failures or disrupt successes. At the same failed state, feedback suppression is more aligned with the response to successful-message transplantation than with a norm-matched random control. Our first ablation tests finite interventions and shows that suppression improves generation, whereas the opposite control degrades it. We construct a negative branch , the reference prediction that guidance extrapolates away from, by increasing I2T feedback. Unlike SAG and PAG, which blur image regions or disrupt attention ( Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ) , this branch preserves the attention computation and gives the current image more influence. Guiding away from it suppresses that influence. We call this control SFG-X. A complementary control, SFG-S, weakens text-to-image conditioning in the same negative branch, so guiding away strengthens conditioning. Together they form Semantic Feedback Guidance (SFG). The in-place variant, iSFG, applies feedback suppression and stronger conditioning directly in the conditional forward, with no extra model evaluations. Early message transplants have the greatest effect on the final outcome, consistent with object layout being largely fixed early in sampling, motivating a SFG guidance window covering the first 20% of image sampling steps. This costs about 1.2 × 1.2\times the base NFE without CFG, compared with 2 × 2\times for an auxiliary branch at every step. SFG corrections remain nearly orthogonal to CFG through sampling, and the two methods combine effectively. Experiments on SD3M, SD3.5M, and FLUX show gains in alignment, preference scores, and distribution quality; transfer to HunyuanVideo improves text-to-video and image-to-video VBench scores over the base model and CFG. Our contributions are: • How I2T feedback preserves image content. Bidirectional transplantation tests the content carried by I2T feedback. Local response analysis and matched two-sided interventions identify suppression as a useful direction on failed trajectories. • A negative branch derived from feedback measurements. SFG-X strengthens I2T feedback in its negative branch and guides against it. SFG combines this control with stronger T2I conditioning; temporal interventions motivate its guidance window. • Branch and in-place controls. iSFG applies the controls directly with zero extra NFE. Experiments evaluate alignment and preference gains, combination with CFG, and transfer to both video tasks.

sections.heading: 2.3 Method: SFG and iSFG
sections.text: SFG combines image-to-text feedback control (SFG-X) with text-to-image conditioning control (SFG-S). It implements both through an auxiliary prediction and an extrapolation step. The in-place variant, iSFG, applies the corresponding message scaling directly within conditional forward pass. Control targets and insertion point. In every joint-attention block, we scale the I2T and T2I messages after softmax and value aggregation, before output projection. TACA and Attend-and-Excite strengthen T2I conditioning ( Lv et al., 2025 ; Chefer et al., 2023 ) ; SFG-X controls the I2T message, which neither method modifies. For a fixed block input, scaling preserves attention logits, joint normalization, and within-modality terms. Model weights stay frozen, but each forward recomputes activations, so earlier edits can affect later blocks through the updated text stream. SFG: auxiliary-branch guidance. sections.heading: 3 Experiments: evaluating mechanism-grounded guidance
sections.text: Tasks, datasets, and metrics. We evaluate text-to-image generation on SD3M, SD3.5M, and FLUX at 1024 2 1024^{2} , and text-to-video and image-to-video generation on HunyuanVideo ( Kong et al., 2024 ) . For images, we evaluate compositional text-image alignment on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and T2I-CompBench++ ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . We report HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) on the same 3,200 images: our evaluation set contains 800 prompts in total across four styles, with four seeds per prompt. We also report FID on COCO for SD3M. For video, we use VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , evaluating seven text-to-video dimensions and eight image-to-video dimensions, and report the aggregate total score for each task. Baselines. Image baselines include PAG ( Ahn et al., 2024 ) , SEG ( Hong, 2024 ) , S 2 -Guidance ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , and TACA ( Lv et al., 2025 ) , with comparisons both without and on top of CFG. TACA strengthens text-to-image conditioning, the reverse information-flow direction from SFG-X, making it a close attention-rebalancing control for SFG-S. We also include Prompt Reinjection, which restores shallow text features ( Yao et al., 2026 ) . Video baselines include CFG, S 2 -Guidance, and CFG-Zero ⋆ ( Fan et al., 2025 ) . Evaluation protocol. Within each configuration, methods share prompts and seeds. GenEval comparisons and guidance-scale sweeps use 553 prompts with six seeds per prompt, giving 3,318 images per configuration. For image benchmark comparisons, the SFG branch runs during the first 20 % 20\% of sampling steps. Sample counts and generation settings appear in App. B , baseline weight sweeps in App. C , and single- and two-object probe diagnostics with separate intervention schedules in App. G . In Tables 1 – 5 , higher scores are better except for FID; bold and underlined values mark the best and second-best results within each model.

sections.heading: 4 Related Work
sections.text: Negative branches and attention strengthening. CFG contrasts conditional and unconditional predictions; training-free self-guidance extrapolates away from a perturbed model prediction ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ; Chung et al., 2025 ; Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ; Hong, 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . SFG-X constructs this reference by strengthening I2T feedback instead of degrading the model through blurred attention, identity maps, or skipped blocks, using the measured response to select the sign. Limited-interval guidance restricts CFG to an empirically chosen interval ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) ; our transplantation experiment measures when feedback most affects the outcome. Attend-and-Excite amplifies neglected subject-token activations ( Chefer et al., 2023 ) . TACA uses a timestep-aware temperature to rebalance cross-modal attention and counter text-token imbalance ( Lv et al., 2025 ) . Both strengthen T2I conditioning, as SFG-S does through guidance, but neither modifies how the image writes back into text. SFG-X instead controls the I2T direction, where our intervention sweeps support suppressing feedback. The two streams of an MMDiT. Studies of MMDiTs examine padding registers, multimodal circuits, prompt reinjection, and attention editing ( Toker et al., 2025 ; Mazur et al., 2026 ; Ge et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) . Toker et al. (2025) find image content in padding tokens; Li et al. (2026) find template tokens maintaining object identity; Shin et al. (2025) identify I2T as the weaker cross-modal direction and build on T2I. We test how the stored content affects generation and find that I2T feedback can preserve errors.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We show that image-to-text feedback in MMDiTs can preserve image content that conflicts with the prompt. Message transplantation, local response analysis, and matched interventions identify feedback suppression as a useful control direction. Building on these findings, SFG guides away from an auxiliary branch with stronger feedback and weaker text-to-image conditioning (about 1.2 × 1.2\times base NFE without CFG), while iSFG applies the corresponding controls directly with zero extra NFE. Experiments across three image backbones demonstrate gains in alignment and preference scores, both without and alongside CFG. The same control strategy improves the evaluated VBench scores in text-to-video and image-to-video generation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Paired sampling protocol
sections.text: For each benchmark and backbone, all baselines and our methods use the same prompts and seed set. Each prompt is generated with multiple seeds before scoring; every generated sample is evaluated, and scores are aggregated according to the benchmark protocol. Methods share the initial noise for each prompt–seed pair, and I2V also fixes the reference image. For each method on a given backbone, we use the same hyperparameters across all applicable benchmarks, with no benchmark-specific tuning. Every hyperparameter-sweep point is evaluated on the full test sets of all applicable benchmarks using the same seed set. Mechanism diagnostics retain their separately stated sampling settings. Seed variability. The reported standard deviations across seeds are 0.031 0.031 for VBench and 0.00332 0.00332 for GenEval, in the same units as their reported overall scores.

sections.heading: F.3 Two-sided sign check
sections.text: Figure 6 in the main text tests whether the same-state sign survives finite interventions and changes final outcomes. Both directions are run at matched strengths on SD3.5M ( cfg = 1 \mathrm{cfg}=1 ; GenEval: 553 prompts with six seeds per prompt, totaling 3,318 images; base 0.3481 0.3481 ), using SFG-X in all joint-attention blocks and with the first- 20 % 20\% schedule. All twelve feedback-suppression settings ( u < 0 u<0 in the auxiliary branch) beat the base; the opposite-sign settings ( u > 0 u>0 ) amplify feedback in the net guidance effect and fall below the base, with lower GenEval scores as ω \omega grows.

sections.heading: Appendix G Single- and two-object omission probes
sections.text: This appendix tests whether image-to-text feedback preserves existing errors and whether suppressing it helps generation recover. We use object-omission probes on single- and two-object prompts to track error signals in the evolving text stream and compare them with final-image outcomes. Without control, warnings tend to persist; with SFG-X, their persistence falls and many warned failures recover. Suppression can also disrupt initially successful outputs, so we measure both effects in the paired cohort: 72.0 % 72.0\% of failures are rescued, whereas 16.7 % 16.7\% of successes are disrupted.

sections.heading: G.1 Probe protocol and paired outcomes

We reuse OSI’s released SD3.5M per-head linear classifiers ( Baek et al., 2026 ) , without retraining: read normalized, projected text keys for noun T5 tokens after the first 77 CLIP tokens, average noun subtokens, then take the median omission probability over the top 100 heads by released accuracy. They span 14 layers (zero-based 9–20, 22, 23). Track each concept separately and probe guided paths on the clean branch at their current latent. All runs use SD3.5M, CFG 1.0, 40 steps, 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 , and SFG-X, with u X = − 0.4 , ω = 8 u_{X}=-0.4,\omega=8 in all joint blocks. The 500-pair run enables steps 1–40 and uses official GenEval Mask2Former evaluation. Its 80 prompts yield 233 single-/267 two-object success/failure pairs and 233/306 concept trajectories (539 total); both seeds receive baseline and guided rollouts. A strict symptom exceeds the step-specific 75th percentile of baseline-success readouts and the paired success readout by at least 0.05. Three consecutive symptomatic steps confirm a warning; onset/confirmation are the first/third step, with medians 8/10. These representations then guide subsequent image updates, raising a question: does this feedback help correct deviations from the prompt, or preserve them? We find that image-to-text (I2T) feedback can preserve the objects and attributes already represented in the evolving image, including errors. Transplanting I2T messages can rescue failures or disrupt successes. At matched intervention strengths, suppressing the influence of I2T feedback improves generation, whereas opposite controls degrade it. These findings motivate Semantic Feedback Guidance (SFG), which suppresses the influence of I2T feedback by guiding away from an auxiliary branch that strengthens this feedback and weakens text-to-image conditioning. The in-place variant, iSFG, directly suppresses I2T feedback and strengthens text-to-image conditioning, requiring no extra model evaluations. Temporal interventions motivate running the SFG branch during the first 20% of image sampling steps, requiring about 1.2 × 1.2\times the base NFE without classifier-free guidance (CFG). Experiments across three image-generation backbones show gains in alignment and preference-model scores. On FLUX, adding SFG to CFG raises GenEval from 0.6661 0.6661 to 0.7479 0.7479 ; on SD3.5M, iSFG adds + 1.33 +1.33 HPSv2.1 over CFG at zero extra NFE. The control also transfers to text-to-video and image-to-video generation, improving VBench scores. Code is available at https://github.com/yyc1215lll-creator/SFG . When dealing with more complex prompts, our method aligns better with the objects and attributes specified in the complex prompts. 1 Introduction Text prompts specify what an image generator should produce, but in MMDiTs, the internal text stream also depends on what the model is drawing. Text queries read image keys and values before later blocks use the updated text stream to condition the image. This image-to-text-to-image loop underlies Stable Diffusion 3/3.5, FLUX, Qwen-Image, and HunyuanVideo ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) . When the image departs from the prompt, does this feedback correct the departure or preserve the existing image content? For the prompt “an apple and an orange,” an image containing only an apple may write that incomplete scene back into the text stream. Figure 2 illustrates the two possible effects: recovering the orange or reinforcing its omission. The answer determines whether early errors are corrected or persist through sampling. Figure 2: Image-to-text feedback. The current image writes into internal text states through B i → t B_{i\rightarrow t} , which later blocks read to update the image. If the image misses an object, does this feedback help recover it or preserve the incomplete scene? Text labels and AI-generated fruit images illustrate schematic states and possible outcomes; the input prompt stays fixed. Existing analyses describe the image-to-text path as a register for image content and object identity, or as the weaker cross-modal direction ( Toker et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Shin et al., 2025 ) . They leave open how this content affects generation. We use image content to mean the objects and attributes represented in the evolving image. Such content can conflict with the prompt; we test the effect of preserving it by intervening on this path. To address these questions, we intervene on the image-to-text path and measure its effect on generation. We find that this feedback can preserve image content that conflicts with the prompt, and identify suppression as a useful direction. Specifically, we design two experiments to examine feedback content and local response direction. Message transplantation shows that feedback can rescue failures or disrupt successes. At the same failed state, feedback suppression is more aligned with the response to successful-message transplantation than with a norm-matched random control. Our first ablation tests finite interventions and shows that suppression improves generation, whereas the opposite control degrades it. We construct a negative branch , the reference prediction that guidance extrapolates away from, by increasing I2T feedback. Unlike SAG and PAG, which blur image regions or disrupt attention ( Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ) , this branch preserves the attention computation and gives the current image more influence. Guiding away from it suppresses that influence. We call this control SFG-X. A complementary control, SFG-S, weakens text-to-image conditioning in the same negative branch, so guiding away strengthens conditioning. Together they form Semantic Feedback Guidance (SFG). The in-place variant, iSFG, applies feedback suppression and stronger conditioning directly in the conditional forward, with no extra model evaluations. Early message transplants have the greatest effect on the final outcome, consistent with object layout being largely fixed early in sampling, motivating a SFG guidance window covering the first 20% of image sampling steps. This costs about 1.2 × 1.2\times the base NFE without CFG, compared with 2 × 2\times for an auxiliary branch at every step. SFG corrections remain nearly orthogonal to CFG through sampling, and the two methods combine effectively. Experiments on SD3M, SD3.5M, and FLUX show gains in alignment, preference scores, and distribution quality; transfer to HunyuanVideo improves text-to-video and image-to-video VBench scores over the base model and CFG. Our contributions are: • How I2T feedback preserves image content. Bidirectional transplantation tests the content carried by I2T feedback. Local response analysis and matched two-sided interventions identify suppression as a useful direction on failed trajectories. • A negative branch derived from feedback measurements. SFG-X strengthens I2T feedback in its negative branch and guides against it. SFG combines this control with stronger T2I conditioning; temporal interventions motivate its guidance window. • Branch and in-place controls. iSFG applies the controls directly with zero extra NFE. Experiments evaluate alignment and preference gains, combination with CFG, and transfer to both video tasks. 2 From mechanism analysis to signed guidance 2.1 Background: guidance and writable MMDiT states CFG extrapolates between conditional and unconditional predictions; training-free self-guidance extrapolates away from a perturbed prediction of the same model. Shading marks steps 1–8. 2.3 Method: SFG and iSFG SFG combines image-to-text feedback control (SFG-X) with text-to-image conditioning control (SFG-S). It implements both through an auxiliary prediction and an extrapolation step. The in-place variant, iSFG, applies the corresponding message scaling directly within conditional forward pass. Control targets and insertion point. In every joint-attention block, we scale the I2T and T2I messages after softmax and value aggregation, before output projection. TACA and Attend-and-Excite strengthen T2I conditioning ( Lv et al., 2025 ; Chefer et al., 2023 ) ; SFG-X controls the I2T message, which neither method modifies. For a fixed block input, scaling preserves attention logits, joint normalization, and within-modality terms. Model weights stay frozen, but each forward recomputes activations, so earlier edits can affect later blocks through the updated text stream. SFG: auxiliary-branch guidance. We evaluate text-to-image generation on SD3M, SD3.5M, and FLUX at 1024 2 1024^{2} , and text-to-video and image-to-video generation on HunyuanVideo ( Kong et al., 2024 ) . For images, we evaluate compositional text-image alignment on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and T2I-CompBench++ ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . We report HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) on the same 3,200 images: our evaluation set contains 800 prompts in total across four styles, with four seeds per prompt. We also report FID on COCO for SD3M. For video, we use VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , evaluating seven text-to-video dimensions and eight image-to-video dimensions, and report the aggregate total score for each task. Baselines. Image baselines include PAG ( Ahn et al., 2024 ) , SEG ( Hong, 2024 ) , S 2 -Guidance ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , and TACA ( Lv et al., 2025 ) , with comparisons both without and on top of CFG. TACA strengthens text-to-image conditioning, the reverse information-flow direction from SFG-X, making it a close attention-rebalancing control for SFG-S. We also include Prompt Reinjection, which restores shallow text features ( Yao et al., 2026 ) . Video baselines include CFG, S 2 -Guidance, and CFG-Zero ⋆ ( Fan et al., 2025 ) . Evaluation protocol. Within each configuration, methods share prompts and seeds. GenEval comparisons and guidance-scale sweeps use 553 prompts with six seeds per prompt, giving 3,318 images per configuration. For image benchmark comparisons, the SFG branch runs during the first 20 % 20\% of sampling steps. Sample counts and generation settings appear in App. B , baseline weight sweeps in App. C , and single- and two-object probe diagnostics with separate intervention schedules in App. G . CFG contrasts conditional and unconditional predictions; training-free self-guidance extrapolates away from a perturbed model prediction ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ; Chung et al., 2025 ; Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ; Hong, 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . SFG-X constructs this reference by strengthening I2T feedback instead of degrading the model through blurred attention, identity maps, or skipped blocks, using the measured response to select the sign. Limited-interval guidance restricts CFG to an empirically chosen interval ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) ; our transplantation experiment measures when feedback most affects the outcome. Attend-and-Excite amplifies neglected subject-token activations ( Chefer et al., 2023 ) . TACA uses a timestep-aware temperature to rebalance cross-modal attention and counter text-token imbalance ( Lv et al., 2025 ) . Both strengthen T2I conditioning, as SFG-S does through guidance, but neither modifies how the image writes back into text. SFG-X instead controls the I2T direction, where our intervention sweeps support suppressing feedback. The two streams of an MMDiT. We test how the stored content affects generation and find that I2T feedback can preserve errors. 5 Conclusion We show that image-to-text feedback in MMDiTs can preserve image content that conflicts with the prompt. Message transplantation, local response analysis, and matched interventions identify feedback suppression as a useful control direction. Building on these findings, SFG guides away from an auxiliary branch with stronger feedback and weaker text-to-image conditioning (about 1.2 × 1.2\times base NFE without CFG), while iSFG applies the corresponding controls directly with zero extra NFE. Experiments across three image backbones demonstrate gains in alignment and preference scores, both without and alongside CFG.
